implementation_notes: C has two distinct meanings and they must not be conflated. static inline: the function has internal linkage and the compiler may inline it; inline alone has no linkage effect in C (unlike C++), it is purely a hint, and a non-static function with the same name in two translation units is a link error. For a header, the portable idiom is 'static inline' (internal linkage, no ODR problem) or, in C99, a plain 'inline' definition plus an 'extern inline' declaration in exactly one .c file to emit the external definition. The optimisation question is separate: -O2 inlines aggressively within a translation unit, and cross-unit inlining requires link-time optimisation (-flto) because the compiler cannot see another .c file's body. Forcing it is __attribute__((always_inline)) (GCC/Clang) or __forceinline (MSVC), and on GCC an always_inline function that cannot be inlined is a compile error, which is a useful safety net.
idiom_name: static inline (internal linkage, the portable header idiom) or __attribute__((always_inline)) to force; -flto for cross-TU
pitfalls: In C, 'inline' has no linkage effect (unlike C++); a non-static inline function defined in two TUs with the same name is a link error - use 'static inline' in a header.
GCC errors if an always_inline function cannot actually be inlined, which is a useful guard; Clang warns instead.
Cross-TU inlining requires -flto (link-time optimisation); the compiler cannot see another .c file's body at compile time, so an inline hint alone does nothing across the boundary.
An 'inline' function whose address is taken is still emitted; the hint then only duplicates the body.
